clinicalPearls: A common, benign, self-limiting hypomelanosis of children and adolescents, widely regarded as a minor or forme fruste manifestation of atopic dermatitis.
Lesions are ill-defined, round to oval, hypopigmented patches with fine powdery scale, most often on the cheeks, lateral upper arms, and shoulders.
It becomes most conspicuous in summer or in darker skin, when the surrounding skin tans and accentuates the pale patches.
The typical evolution is from a faintly erythematous scaly stage to a residual hypopigmented, minimally scaly patch that gradually resolves.
Wood's lamp shows only mild accentuation with partial preservation of pigment, in contrast to the sharp bright-white of vitiligo.
It is a clinical diagnosis; scrapings for fungal microscopy help exclude pityriasis versicolor when there is diagnostic doubt.
Hypopigmentation reflects post-inflammatory reduction in melanin and disturbed melanosome transfer, not melanocyte destruction.
Management centres on emollients, gentle skin care, sun protection, and reassurance, with low-potency topical anti-inflammatories for troublesome cases.
reference.pathophysiology: Pityriasis alba represents a low-grade, subclinical dermatitis, most commonly within the atopic spectrum, that culminates in post-inflammatory hypopigmentation. Mild eczematous inflammation and associated dryness disturb the orderly transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes and reduce the number and size of active melanosomes, while the overlying hyperkeratosis and scale scatter incident light and further diminish apparent pigmentation. Melanocytes are preserved but functionally quiescent, which is why repigmentation eventually occurs spontaneously. Ultraviolet exposure deepens the contrast by tanning the unaffected surrounding skin. Xerosis, frequent washing, sun exposure, and an atopic diathesis are recognised contributory factors, and the condition is regarded as one of the minor diagnostic criteria of atopic dermatitis.
additionalInvestigations: Skin scraping with potassium hydroxide microscopy to exclude pityriasis versicolor and dermatophytosis
Wood's lamp examination showing mild, incomplete accentuation
Dermoscopy revealing fine white scale and preserved pigment network
Skin biopsy reserved for atypical, persistent, or treatment-resistant lesions to exclude hypopigmented mycosis fungoides
Assessment for other features of atopic dermatitis
Serial review to confirm gradual spontaneous resolution
redFlags: Persistence into adulthood or lesions that fail to resolve, prompting reconsideration of hypopigmented mycosis fungoides
Progressive, atrophic, or indurated plaques suggesting morphoea or lymphoma
Sharply demarcated, truly depigmented macules indicating vitiligo
Widespread scaly lesions with positive mycology pointing to a fungal infection
reference.prognosis: Pityriasis alba is entirely benign and self-limiting, with pigmentation returning spontaneously over months to a few years, though relapses are common during childhood. It carries no long-term sequelae and requires only supportive care and reassurance.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for vitiligo and causing undue alarm or inappropriate treatment
Overlooking pityriasis versicolor by not performing mycological examination in scaly cases
Attributing persistent adult lesions to pityriasis alba and missing hypopigmented mycosis fungoides
Neglecting the underlying atopic dryness, so that emollient therapy is omitted
Promising rapid resolution and undermining confidence when repigmentation is inevitably slow
